summary: The note describes how the term "solar tsunami", coined by astrophysicist Dr. Lia Rodriguez on September 21, 2023 for massive solar flares and coronal mass ejections, became a pop culture phenomenon. It traces the idea through film, music, fashion, video games, education and marketing between October 2023 and early 2024. The note closes by saying sociologists see the trend as comparable to the space race's cultural influence.
one_line: A solar event dubbed a "solar tsunami" in September 2023 spawned a wave of films, music, fashion, games, education and marketing.
key_facts: Dr. Lia Rodriguez, an astrophysicist, announced detection of an unprecedented solar event on September 21, 2023 and playfully called it a "solar tsunami".
In Rodriguez's press release, solar tsunamis are massive solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) rippling out from the sun, like waves from a pebble thrown into a pond.
The scientific community was interested in the potential impact on satellite communications and power grids.
Michael Firestone, a real estate mogul turned director, announced on November 5 that he was fast-tracking the film "Tsunami from the Sun".
Indie singer Lyra Celestia released her hit single "Solar Tsunami" on December 21, and it became a global anthem.
By December, charts had titles like "Flares and Beats," "Wave of Fire," and "Tsunami Drops", and DJs used names like "DJ Coronal Mass" and "Plasma Wave".
French designer Francoise Rocher won acclaim at New York Fashion Week in January 2024 for her "Celestial Fury" line using thermochromic fabrics that change color with heat.
The video game "Solar Surge" is a survivalist hit set on a spaceship navigating the aftermath of a CME.
The mobile strategy game "Tidal Sun" has the tagline "Catch the Wave, Save the Day".
The "Supercharged Science" YouTube series gained millions of views with solar tsunami simulations and experiments.
Students from Silicon Valley's FutureGen Academy built a basketball court-sized, sensor-driven wave pool replicating solar waves for a science fair.
The brand SolWave released a solar charger claimed to use "the same principles that powered solar storms", a claim the note says any astrophysicist would chuckle at.
Ads used the tagline "Ride the Solar Wave", and some people criticized the commercialism.
The note says the Sun is 93 million miles away.
